name: GentleMax Pro

lead: GentleMax Pro is a Candela clinic laser that combines two wavelengths, alexandrite (755 nm) and Nd:YAG (1064 nm). It is mainly used to reduce facial and body hair for cleaner, less hairy skin, and also lists pigmented and vascular lesions.

Light absorbed by melanin in the hair heats and damages the follicle. Alexandrite is used across skin types and Nd:YAG is generally used on darker skin, which is the reason for pairing both in one machine. Studies naming this device are mostly small clinical series and safety reports, including a retrospective review of use on children after ear reconstruction.

paras: It is a professional device used by dermatology and aesthetic practices, with treatment typically spread over many sessions. Clinics choose the setting that suits the person's skin and hair type. Light or fine hair responds poorly, and in looksmaxxing circles it comes up mainly for facial hair reduction.

Reported effects include redness, swelling, acne flares, colour changes, burns and, rarely, a delayed hives-like rash after alexandrite epilation. Outcomes depend on skin and hair type and the operator.

angle.text: GentleMax Pro uses alexandrite and Nd:YAG light to heat follicles so hair growth reduces over sessions, giving cleaner, less hairy facial and body skin across skin tones. Studies naming the device are small, alongside the broad hair-removal literature.

lead: GentleMax Pro is a clinic laser platform made by Candela that combines a 755-nm alexandrite laser with a 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser in one device. It is used by dermatology and aesthetic practices, most commonly for laser hair removal, and its listed study conditions also include pigmented lesions, vascular lesions and pseudofolliculitis barbae (razor bumps).[1][2] In looksmaxxing culture it falls under the hardmaxx category of professional procedures, usually discussed in connection with facial hair reduction.

Laser hair removal works by selective photothermolysis: light absorbed by melanin in the hair heats and damages the follicle while sparing most surrounding skin.[3] Reference sources describe alexandrite (755 nm) as used across skin types and Nd:YAG (1064 nm) as the option generally used on darker skin, which is the rationale for pairing the two wavelengths in one machine.[3]

Published studies that name the device are mostly small clinical series and safety reports rather than large controlled trials. They include a retrospective review of its use on children after ear reconstruction[1], a large clinic review of an uncommon delayed hives-like reaction after alexandrite epilation[4], and registered manufacturer-sponsored evaluations.[2][5]
infobox: Clinic laser platform (alexandrite 755 nm plus Nd:YAG 1064 nm)
Hair removal; pigmented and vascular lesions

paras: The device pairs two wavelengths: 755-nm alexandrite and 1064-nm Nd:YAG.[1] Alexandrite is generally listed as suitable for all skin types in hair-removal references, while Nd:YAG is the wavelength generally used for darker skin because it is less absorbed by epidermal melanin.[3] A Plus variant has also been registered in clinical evaluations.[2][5]

Laser hair removal works best on dark, coarse hair, and reference sources note that light, red, grey or white hair and fine vellus hair respond poorly. Most people need at least eight treatments spaced several weeks apart, and regulators define permanent reduction as a long-term, stable reduction in regrowing hairs rather than total removal.[3] Registered evaluations of GentleMax Pro list unwanted hair, unwanted fine facial hair and pseudofolliculitis barbae as conditions studied.[2][5]

Registered evaluations also list pigmented and vascular lesions.[2] In published case work, a multi-modal laser approach that included lasers of this type was reported for glomangiomas, and the alexandrite laser has been used to remove hair-bearing skin on reconstructed ears in children.[1][6]

General laser hair removal references list itching, redness and swelling lasting a few days as common, with acne flares, skin colour changes, burns, scabbing, bruising and infection reported less often.[3] A retrospective study of 13,284 patients treated with Candela alexandrite systems, including GentleMax, described a delayed, persistent urticarial (hives-like) rash as an uncommon side effect.[4]
Within hardmaxx discussion the platform is mentioned as one of the brand-name machines offered by clinics for facial hair reduction. No forum or community sources are summarised here.

Published evidence that names GentleMax Pro is limited to small or retrospective reports. A retrospective chart review described the 755-nm GentleMax Pro in children following auricular reconstruction.[1] A retrospective study of 13,284 epilation patients, treated with GentleLase-family and GentleMax devices, characterised a delayed urticaria side effect over extended follow-up.[4] Registered manufacturer-sponsored trials include NCT04993066, a completed 77-participant safety and efficacy evaluation of GentleMax Pro Plus, and NCT04975243, a 20-participant study on unwanted fine facial hair.[2][5] Results of these registrations are not summarised in the registry entries cited here.
